newsitem.title: UK: Cameroon plans new measures to boost cocoa quality.
newsitem.headline: Cameroon plans new measures to boost cocoa quality.

text.p: Cameroon, West Africa's third biggest cocoa producer, is contemplating new measures to boost cocoa quality in response to concerns that arose after it liberalised its market six years ago.

Hope Sona Ebai, director general of the National Cocoa and Coffee Board, said the board, stripped of its power to oversee the quality of exports in 1991, was looking at ways in which private enterprises can be strengthened to take over the role.

"We are studying ways to put upcountry controls so we can eliminate (poor quality cocoa) from the marketing chain early on. But this has to be done in the privatisation context," Ebai told reporters on the fringes of a meeting of the International Cocoa Organisation (ICCO).
The aim was to regain the confidence of exporters and buyers in the local system so that forward sales, which constituted the majority of Cameroon's cocoa sales in the past, could be restored.
The bulk of Cameroon's cocoa was sold up to a year in advance before the liberalisation when the board acted as a shock absorber, providing guarantee for low-interest bank credits for exporters.
Now most of the country's produce is sold in the spot market.
Cameroon cocoa has a higher butter to bean content and before the liberalisation commanded a premium over the Ivorian produce.
But that premium has now disappeared in line with the drop in quality which Ebai said was a consequence of the "lack of risk management tools".

One problem is that the number of exporters have snowballed to 375 from about a dozen before the World Bank-sponsored liberalisation programme began. Each exporter also employs several upcountry buyers.

The scores of exporters chasing business has triggered a rush for produce. This put tremendous pressure on farmers to gather cocoa faster. They were often asked to skip the fermentation process, which takes about six days, and drying was done inappropriately, Ebai said.
To solve the problem the marketing board is now considering making the licensing process more stringent for exporters, possibly by introducing minimum investment requirements.
"At the moment if you have a business bag you can become a cocoa trader," said Ebai.

Another way to tackle the problem was to extend the powers of exporter unions so that they can introduce sanctions on the trade. They were also considering setting up a mutual fund to guarantee export contracts.
Ebai said buyers had now become more selective and opened up offices in Douala, the country's main port, to check quality before signing purchasing contracts.

A cocoa zone was covered more intensively as a result of stiff local competition for business and this could lead to higher production in the future, although he did not expect export levels to increase.

Cameroon's 1996/97 harvest, which is now entirely sold, is estimated at 120,000 tonnes. There is one local processing plant which has a maximum capacity of 25,000 tonnes but currently processes about 10,000-15,000 tonnes a year.
